newsitem.title: SPAIN: Interest in Spain short-term debt should revive.
newsitem.headline: Interest in Spain short-term debt should revive.

text.p: Investors will likely resume buying Spanish short-term paper after a key U.S. interest rate decision next week, attracted by its resilience in the face of EMU jitters, analysts said.
Before moving ahead with new buying in the short end, Spanish dealers would rather await the Federal Reserve's March 25 decision on whether to raise U.S. interest rates.
"The most attractive is the one-year, which will suffer the least from any European Monetary Union (EMU) delay," said Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

One- to three-year bond prices dropped sharply in recent days on profit-taking and analysts said this segment should now offer the best value in coming months as it is the most resistant to European single currency worries.
One-year bills were trading on Thursday at a yield of around 5.60 percent. Yields were unchanged at 5.59 percent at a bi-monthly auction. The bills hit a record low at 5.172 percent in mid-February.
"Before people were playing the curve pricing in a rate cut. So we had a drastic profit-taking after the Bank of Spain cut its official rate on Friday," a money market dealer said.
Last Friday, the Bank of Spain sanctioned its second rate cut in the year, cutting 25 basis points to 5.75 percent. It was the 10th rate cut since December 1995.
Other dealers said the market is not expecting any further easing of credit for the moment.
The yield on the June one-year MIBOR future contract was trading on Thursday at around 5.70 percent.
"At present, current market rates up to three-year maturities are not expecting cuts anymore," said another dealer.
The three-year benchmark 9.4 percent April 1999 was trading on Thursday at around 106.51/58, yielding 5.97 percent.
It was recovering from 6.02 percent a day earlier but it was still above level at around 5.60 percent one week ago on the eve of the last Bank of Spain's official cut.
Traders were confident the correction was almost over.
"This correction has already found a top. I expect all the maturities from one-year to three-year to offer good value," said Emilio Sainz at Natwest in Madrid.
Dealers said a rise in the three-year bond yield should be capped at 6.25 percent.
"In any case I'd buy it at that level," said one trader who asked not to be named.
"Before Wednesday I expect the market to remain unchanged. But after that, it seems to me the Spanish yield curve should start steepening again," he added.

Expectations of a continued positive trend in CPI, seen falling toward 2.0 percent year-on-year in May from February's 2.5 percent should boost market confidence in further monetary easing, dealers said.
